transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-01-15 16:00 UTC · Duration: ~58 mins
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Emily (AtlasAnalytics Head of ML), Ravi (Platform), Laura (Product)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): Kickoff to scope POC for AtlasAnalytics. Focus: traffic profile (steady qps + spikes), input/output token mix, latency vs cost tradeoffs, plan benchmarks and deliverables.

[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — we have Diego from SE, and on the Atlas side Emily, Ravi, and Laura, right?
[00:10] Emily Chen: Yep that's right, hi hi.
[00:13] Ravi Singh: Hello.
[00:15] Diego Ramos: Hi all.
[00:17] Maya Patel: Cool. The goal for today is to lock down the workload characteristics and agree on success criteria and the benchmark cadence for the POC. We'll also capture any security blockers for Private evaluation. Sound good?
[00:29] Laura Park: Yes, sounds good. We want a relatively narrow scope — prove we can handle our core inference path first.
[00:36] Emily Chen: To add context — our prod traffic is mostly user chat completions inside our analytics UI. Baseline steady QPS is roughly 80 QPS globally, with regional peaks hitting 600 QPS during reporting windows. There's also a daily 10–15 min burst pattern when reports run.
[00:50] Maya Patel: Nice, that's helpful. Can you share average prompt and response sizes?
[00:55] Emily Chen: Avg prompt is about 110–140 input tokens, output around 200–300 tokens. But there is long-tail — some autosummarize flows push outputs to 1k tokens.
[01:07] Diego Ramos: Okay, so token mix roughly 1:2 input:output for the common path, with tail cases higher. That matters for batching and KV cache usage.
[01:18] Ravi Singh: Also our svcs are in a VPC and we have strict egress policy; if Private, we'd need peering and a cert fingerprinting. For hosted we need data residency for EU users.
[01:30] Maya Patel: Understood. Security & compliance we'll capture — Emily, can you confirm SOC2 scope and whether any of this needs to be HIPAA?
[01:37] Emily Chen: Not HIPAA, but SOC2 + GDPR controls are must-haves.
[01:41] Maya Patel: Great. For success criteria, how does p95 latency under 250ms for simple prompts sound as a target? And cost target — do you have a per-token budget?
[01:51] Laura Park: Latency is important for interactive flows. 250ms p95 is aggressive but ideal. For cost we are modeling ~ $0.40–0.60 per 1k combined tokens as acceptable for hosted, and if Dedicated gets us below that with our committed traffic, we'll consider it.
[02:06] Emily Chen: Also want predictable tail behavior during bursts — 90th to 99th percentile mustn't blow up.
[02:12] Diego Ramos: Cool. Technically, for benchmarking we'll want to profile both steady-state and burst scenarios: steady at 80 QPS, regional peak simulation to 600 QPS, and stress bursts up to 1k QPS for short windows to test autoscale. We'll capture p50/p95/p99, cost per token, and throughput per GPU. For the model we recommend starting with a quantized 2.7B variant (internal name: redwood-2.7q) to match-ish capability and then try a larger 7B quantized variant for quality spot checks.
[02:45] Emily Chen: Is quantized performance parity good enough for us? We worry about hallucination/regression.
[02:51] Diego Ramos: We'll pair with Redwood Optimize metrics — run a small eval set you provide to compare quality delta between quantized and float. If regression > 3% on your eval metrics we can try a higher quality variant.
[03:03] Laura Park: What's the recommended concurrency per instance?
[03:07] Diego Ramos: With continuous batching the runtime picks a batching window based on request arrival. For short prompts you can get high concurrency per GPU — e.g., a single A100-equivalent can handle several hundred tokens throughput, but this depends heavily on sequence length. We'll capture tokens/sec and effective concurrency in the run.
[03:24] Ravi Singh: For our platform, noisy neighbor isolation is a concern. If we go hosted, we want route-level isolation or some capacity reservation.
[03:33] Maya Patel: Right — Dedicated would give predictable capacity and isolation, and Private would put the control plane in your VPC. We'll include both scenarios in the pricing worksheet.
[03:41] Emily Chen: How about warm vs cold cache? A lot of our queries re-use similar prefixes — sentence rephrases — would KV cache help?
[03:48] Diego Ramos: Yes, prefix and KV caching can reduce compute a lot. We'll instrument cache hits in the benchmark; if your warmed prefix hit rate is high (say >30%) you can reduce token compute costs significantly. We'll need a sample of repeated sessions to measure that.
[04:02] Laura Park: We'll anonymize and share sample logs.
[04:05] Maya Patel: Perfect. Now, about telemetry — what CSV fields do you need for the workload?
[04:10] Diego Ramos: Ideally: timestamp, region, input_token_count, output_token_count, latency_ms, request_type (summarize/chat/insight), user_id_hash, outcome (ok/error). If you can't provide user hashes, timestamps + request_type + token counts are fine.
[04:23] Emily Chen: We can export that — we'll redact any PII.
[04:26] Diego Ramos: Great. For benchmark plan: step 1 baseline run (hosted, quantized model): 80 QPS steady for 30m to validate steady-state. Step 2 surge testing: 10x bursts to 600 QPS for 15m windows, and a short stress up to 1k QPS for 5m to validate autoscale/fallbacks. Step 3 evaluate Dedicated with same traffic to compare p95/compute cost.
[04:49] Maya Patel: Good. Who owns scheduling the runs?
[04:52] Emily Chen: We'll coordinate but would like Diego to kick off the hosted baseline using our sample prompt set.
[04:57] Diego Ramos: Yep I can do that — I'll need the sample prompt pack and the token distribution file.
[05:02] Ravi Singh: Also add that our SLs require audit logs for all inference requests for a 90-day retention for EU tenants.
[05:10] Maya Patel: We'll include the audit log solution in the SOW; for hosted we can provide audit exports, and Private will give you full control.
[05:17] Laura Park: Regarding timelines — we want a POC to be wrapped in 4 weeks, with benchmarks in week 1–2 and quality evals week 3, decision week 4. Is that feasible?
[05:27] Diego Ramos: Aggressive but doable if we get data quickly. The key path is sample traffic + eval set — once we have that we can run tests and provide results in 48–72 hours for each test.
[05:38] Emily Chen: Okay we'll target sending data by Monday (2025-01-20).
[05:43] Maya Patel: Great. One more question — do you have a target for cold-start latency for new sessions?
[05:48] Ravi Singh: We want cold-start p95 under 500ms ideally, but we know that's harder.
[05:54] Diego Ramos: Cold-start depends on model sharding and setup. We'll measure end-to-end cold p95 including network. If needed we can recommend pre-warmed pools to hit your target at an added cost.
[06:05] Laura Park: If Dedicated reduces the cold-start problem that's a plus.
[06:09] Maya Patel: For evaluation metrics we'll produce a benchmark report with p50/p95/p99 latencies, tokens/sec, cost per token, failure/error rate, and quality deltas on your eval set.
[06:20] Emily Chen: Sounds good. For quality delta, we'll use our internal rouge-like autometric and a small human spot-check sample.
[06:27] Diego Ramos: Perfect. We'll run the first baseline with redwood-2.7q, then run a comparison with redwood-7bq and floating variant if needed.
[06:36] Maya Patel: Any concerns about model compatibility — do you use tool-calls or structured outputs?
[06:41] Emily Chen: Mostly freeform natural language outputs; small percent use structured JSON responses for downstream ingestion.
[06:47] Diego Ramos: We'll test the structured outputs as part of the QA pass; function-calling support is available on the hosted API.
[06:54] Ravi Singh: About data residency — some EU tenant traffic must stay in eu-central. Can Redwood route per-region?
[06:59] Maya Patel: Yes we can route by policy; for hosted we'll pin region endpoints; Dedicated can be regionally provisioned.
[07:06] Laura Park: Okay. Anything else on the scope?
[07:09] Emily Chen: One thing: our cost models assume average of 400 tokens per request. If the cost is higher than expected we'll need to consider stronger quantization or more aggressive caching.
[07:20] Diego Ramos: We'll include estimated cost curves in the proposal. Also note that batching tradeoffs can reduce cost but increase latency; we'll show cost-vs-latency curves from the runs.
[07:31] Maya Patel: Quick note on fallbacks — we have model variants and routing policies to failover to a lower-cost model if SLO is at risk. We'll include that strategy.
[07:40] Emily Chen: Excellent.
[07:42] Laura Park: When do you need the security docs?
[07:45] Maya Patel: We'll send our SOC2 whitepaper and security checklist immediately after this call. Ravi, you said you'll confirm any extra cert requirements?
[07:54] Ravi Singh: Yes I'll list out the firewall/IP ranges and cert fingerprint needs by 2025-01-21.
[07:59] Diego Ramos: I'll prepare the benchmark scripts and a load signature template so your infra team can see what we'll run.
[08:06] Maya Patel: Great — to recap next steps: Maya sends SOW & pricing, Diego runs hosted baseline after receiving sample prompts, Emily shares telemetry and eval set, Ravi confirms security reqs. We'll tentatively schedule the 1-hour benchmark for 2025-01-24.
[08:20] Emily Chen: That all sounds good.
[08:22] Maya Patel: Any final questions?
[08:24] Laura Park: No, thanks.
[08:25] Ravi Singh: All good.
[08:27] Diego Ramos: Thanks everyone — I'll follow up with the load script and run plan.
[08:31] Maya Patel: Thanks all, we'll follow up in email with attachments.
